author: allafrica
title: Zimbabwe Gradually Maintains Foreign Currencies Amid Gold‑Backed Currency Roll‑Out
text: Zimbabwe Gradually Maintains Foreign Currencies Amid Gold‑Backed Currency Roll‑Out The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe has affirmed it will not rush to abandon foreign currencies while it introduces the gold‑backed Zimbabwe Gold (ZiG), a new domestic money designed to replace the inflation‑ridden old dollar. The central bank said the transition will be gradual, market‑driven and will only happen once necessary conditions are met. Early trading of ZiG has shown modest appreciation against the U.S. dollar, with banks and traders eagerly converting the old local currency. The policy mirrors Zimbabwe's 2009 multi‑currency arrangement and signals a cautious approach to restoring confidence in the economy. In a recent announcement, the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe has clarified that there is no immediate plan to abandon foreign currencies as part of the country's ongoing currency transition. The statement was issued amidst growing uncertainty over when and how Zimbabwe will exit its long‑standing multi‑currency regime, which was adopted in 2009 after a period of hyperinflation that had deeply eroded confidence in the local currency. The deputy governor of the central bank, Dr. Innocent Matshe, explained that all actions will be \"market driven\" and that a number of preconditions must be satisfied before any eventual shift to a single domestic currency can be implemented.ZiG Launch Reassures Market StakeholdersThis stance aims to reassure businesses and the general public that contracts, foreign‑currency holdings, and day‑to‑day transactions will not be disrupted abruptly. The announcement follows the launch of the Zimbabwe Gold (ZiG), a gold‑backed local currency that was unveiled in April 2024. The ZiG was introduced to replace the old Zimbabwean dollar, which had become obsolescent due to extreme inflation.In its first week of trading the new coin gained 1.1 percent against the U.S. dollar as global gold prices climbed amid geopolitical tensions. Bank traders and businesses welcomed the currency, and several institutions successfully converted the old local currency into the new gold‑backed standard. Despite this early positive reception, the central bank has made clear that ZiG will not immediately displace the dollar. Instead, it will circulate alongside foreign currencies until 2030, giving the economy time to adjust.This approach is intended to maintain confidence among investors and workers whose wages have been eroded by inflation. African policy analysts note that the gradual transition mirrors Zimbabwe's earlier strategy of maintaining foreign currency alongside a domestic issue. In the 2009 multi‑currency system, the U.S. dollar was a legal tender, and the country later reintroduced a local denomination while preserving foreign money in circulation.The RBZ deputy governor reiterated that the shift to a mono‑currency economy will be phased and will only occur when the market conditions are suitable. He also highlighted the importance of stable gold prices, noting that a 2026 sale of gold coins undertaken in April to counter rising gold costs had negligible economic impact. The central bank's decision to hold off on a swift move to the ZiG demonstrates a cautious approach, aimed at preventing market shock.Zimbabwe Currency Transition Balancing ActThis measured stance resonates with stakeholders who have historically been wary of abrupt currency changes that can cause significant financial loss. Overall, Zimbabwe's currency strategy illustrates a balancing act: the need to re‑price an economy that still relies heavily on U.S. dollar and other foreign currencies, while attempting to re‑establish a credible, gold‑backed domestic money that can combat inflation and restore trust among the populace.Through a deliberate schedule that will span until 2030, the Reserve Bank's cautious policy signals a commitment to preserving market stability and encouraging confidence in both the new ZiG and existing foreign funds. The global community and local investors will be watching closely as Zimbabweo attempts to construct a financial framework that can navigate the challenges of hyperinflation, currency volatility, and long‑term economic recovery.
